data.title: US seeks answers on Nvidiaâs sale of chips to China: Bessent
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] The US is seeking answers from Nvidia on its chip sales to China and will find out who was in charge of compliance at the company formerly led by Jensen Huang, who resigned following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday (Nov 22).

“We’ve been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers.... It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent told the CBS programme Face the Nation.

Reports about Huang’s relationship with a woman whom US intelligence suspects of being ​a Chinese spy and his extramarital affair with a company executive led to his resignation and investigations by US regulators and the FBI, congressional action, an internal review and a proposed investor class-action lawsuit.

Days after Huang’s resignation, President Donald Trump’s administration issued a rule to further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia, tightening controls ahead of Trump’s trip to China last week for talks with President Xi Jinping.

Bessent said the chipmaker’s board of directors is working to determine what had happened, and he expressed confidence that it would “come up with some very fulsome and robust answers.”

“We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there,” Bessent said. “We will see which level of the business knew about this. Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle level? Did it go all the way to the top?”

Trump said on Friday that he would like to see Huang apologise and return to Nvidia. Asked whether he agreed with Trump, Bessent said more information is needed.

“I think we have to see where the buck stops,” Bessent said.

Nvidia board Chairman Harvey Jones has said the board will not rehire Huang. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Trump-Xi-Putin summit marks the start of the post-Western order
data.description:
AMERICAN presidents who lose a midterm election have a habit of boarding Air Force One soon afterwards.

In November 2014, a week after the Democrats lost the Senate, Barack Obama flew to Beijing for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.

Obama returned with a landmark climate agreement with Chinese President Xi Jinping, longer visas for students and business travellers, a deal to scrap tariffs on high-tech products and new military confidence-building measures.

Twenty years earlier, after the Republican landslide of 1994, Bill Clinton went to Bogor, Indonesia, where Apec leaders committed to free and open trade across the Pacific.

Neither trip rescued their fortunes at home. But Americans got something out of them.

Donald Trump, whose party lost both chambers of Congress on Nov 3, followed the script and flew to Shenzhen. If he brought anything for Americans, it is much harder to find.

Symbolism over substance

What the world will remember from the Nov 19 trilateral summit is a photograph.

At Kylin Villa, Xi sat at the centre of the table, with the presidents of the United States and Russia on either side.

Chinese diplomacy has always understood that power is also a matter of staging, and this was a masterpiece of the genre: China as the Middle Kingdom, convening and steadying the world.

The country that built the post-1945 order sat on one flank, at the same level as Russia, an economy of roughly US$2.9 trillion – against America’s US$32.6 trillion – with a declining population and a war in Ukraine approaching its fifth year with no end in sight.

If historians need one image to mark the start of the post-Western order, Shenzhen has supplied it.

Trump rated the summit “12 out of 10”. Analysts around the world are less generous.

Their near-unanimous verdict is that the meeting was heavy on symbolism and light on substance. I can only agree.

An ironic peace declaration

Trump, Xi and Vladmir Putin talked for about 90 minutes. No breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran. No mention of Taiwan. There was no movement on the rare earth metals Beijing continues to ration, and no arms control was discussed.

The meeting produced a “Declaration toward Peace” that looks as if the surrealist painter Salvador Dali had composed it on an off day: United Nations reform, oil barrels, immunity of heads of state, and nuclear risks.

Tommy Koh, diplomat and Singapore’s former permanent representative to the UN, has called the declaration “absurd”.

It is curious that UN reform has suddenly become a shared priority for three veto powers that have spent decades blocking any change to the Security Council.

Are the three powers signalling an agreement on who should succeed Antonio Guterres, whose term ends in December, as next UN secretary-general?

The second point, a pledge to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products “for the benefit of all nations”, is presented as energy security.

In practice it is a gift to the Kremlin, whose war economy depends on hydrocarbon revenues that have fallen sharply in 2026.

The most troubling is the third point.

The three leaders declared that state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials are “of paramount importance” and that the International Criminal Court and similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction”.

The language serves Putin perfectly: the court issued a warrant for his arrest in 2023 over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children. A declaration about peace has turned into a declaration about impunity.

Only the fourth point deserves its place under the title.

The three presidents reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, the formula Reagan and Gorbachev adopted in 1985, and promised a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

The wording is careful. It speaks of “risks” rather than arms control, which China rejects while it expands its arsenal. It focuses on proliferation, the one issue on which those who already have the bomb always agree.

The message for Asia and Asean

Some experts suspect Moscow and Beijing are thinking less about Iran than about Japan and South Korea deciding one day that the American umbrella can no longer be trusted.

That is the real message for Asia. Tokyo and Seoul watched their protector sit in a lakeside villa with their two main strategic adversaries, in a meeting that ran twice as long as Trump’s session with the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi insisted Japan’s interests would not be compromised, while her officials privately questioned Washington’s commitment.

In Seoul, scholars talk openly of the pillars of national security policy being shaken.

After 70 years of loyalty, America’s closest Asian allies may conclude that they have been thrown under the bus, and that the bus is Chinese.

For South-east Asia, and for Singapore in particular, Shenzhen is a warning more than a shock.

This region has prospered in a world where rules, however imperfect, constrained the strong.

A concert of three powers that dismisses international courts and treats the UN as a matter to settle among themselves is the opposite of what middle powers and small states need.

At the Apec table, Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong urged the region to keep cooperating even when it cannot agree on everything, and to resist splitting into rival blocs. That is the right instinct.

With Singapore chairing Asean next year, the task is to give real substance to coalitions of middle powers and to keep Asean at the centre of regional diplomacy, so that South-east Asia stays in the room rather than on the menu.

Obama came home from Beijing with a climate deal.

Clinton came home from Bogor with a trade vision.

Trump came home from Shenzhen with a photograph, and the photograph belongs to Xi.

The writer is vice-dean (executive education) and associate professor in practice at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, National University of Singapore

data.title: Procter & Gamble to increase factory shifts without humans to cut costs
data.description:
CONSUMER product giant Procter & Gamble says it plans to increase the number of factories that can run shifts without human intervention over the next several years as a way to increase productivity and save up to US$10 billion.

The Cincinnati-based maker of Gillette razors, Tide Pods and Crest toothpaste has invested heavily in recent years in automated manufacturing lines that can run unattended for several hours at a time, often in the overnight hours. P&G currently operates 15 such sites around the world and plans to add more in 2027.

“We are taking unattended operations to a whole new level,” Luc Reynaert, chief product supply officer, said on Thursday (Nov 19) in a presentation to investors in Cincinnati.

Procter & Gamble has also deployed autonomous robots at loading docks and in warehouses, and has experimented with driverless trucks. Reynaert said unattended operations will improve manufacturing productivity by up to 20 per cent over the next four years.

But the rise of so-called dark-shift manufacturing has provoked fears of enormous job losses.

In a speech in June at the United Auto Workers quadrennial constitutional convention, the union’s president, Shawn Fain, called robots replacing humans in factories a “profound threat.”

Josh Bivens, chief economist at the Economic Policy Institute, a pro-labour think tank, said unattended factories were “not the thing that keeps me up at night,” because it’s difficult to stop automation once companies begin making upgrades.

He said the United States should increase its social safety net to better cover workers displaced by such technological advances.

Procter & Gamble had its first unattended shift at a Gillette factory in Berlin in 2024. The plant now runs without technicians during the hard-to-staff overnight shift, freeing up employees to focus on less-repetitive tasks or jobs in which they interact with customers during the day.

Procter & Gamble executives said unattended shifts give workers better schedules and allow them to focus on consumer-facing tasks, but acknowledged that they will need leaner teams. On Thursday, the company said it would cut its product-supply workforce, which includes contractors, by 20 per cent to 30 per cent by 2030.

Product-supply jobs at the company include roles in manufacturing, purchasing, planning, engineering and quality control. Roughly 65,000 workers fall into that category. However, a company spokesperson said the reductions have been underway for a few years as part of a supply-chain improvement program called Supply 3.0. NYTIMES

data.title: Nvidiaâs slump, Anthropicâs listing turn spotlight on Big AIâs need for new governance frameworks
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] When news of Jensen Huang’s extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive broke earlier this month, it surprised me that many observers seemed to think he had finally crossed the line.

It was already clear by then that Huang had also been having an affair with a woman US authorities believed was a Chinese spy, and that he had misrepresented the nature of that relationship to senior officials at Nvidia for some time.

In my view, this was objectively much worse than an illicit dalliance with a subordinate. The alleged spy was linked to a major buyer of Nvidia chips in Singapore called Megaspeed, which had ties to Chinese companies. This naturally alarmed the US government, and has already led to tighter restrictions on Nvidia.

Last week, the US Commerce Department announced licence requirements for the export of advanced artificial intelligence chips for use in data centres providing remote computing power to China. Licence requirements were also slapped on the export of advanced AI chips to destinations with “unacceptable risk of diversion” – including Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil and Thailand.

These restrictions and the ouster of Huang – who had advocated for China to be allowed access to AI chips, and provided buyers of AI chips with financial support – have felt like a supply shock for the booming technology sector.

Nvidia’s shares sank a further 22.9 per cent last week, despite the company reporting robust third-quarter financial numbers and strong revenue guidance for 2027. Since the end of last month, when the spy scandal began making headlines, Nvidia’s shares have slumped 38.7 per cent.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have fallen 8.8 per cent and 11.8 per cent, respectively, during the same period.

“Indispensable” CEOs

To be clear, I’m not suggesting that Huang should be excused for his affairs with employees of Nvidia – it later emerged that there was more than one.

Illicit relationships with customers, business partners or subordinates are effectively undisclosed conflicts of interests that have the potential to harm a company and its stakeholders. One might also argue that such lapses reveal character flaws that make CEOs unsuited for their roles.

Certainly, cultural attitudes towards this sort of behaviour seem to have become less forgiving. In recent years, major companies such as Nestle, BP, McDonald’s and Intel have given their CEOs the boot for relationships with subordinates.

Yet, Huang’s involvement with the alleged Chinese spy clearly had the potential to cause far more damage to Nvidia and its stakeholders than his affairs with employees – not least by putting all of them in the crosshairs of the US government.

This case is also perplexing as Huang’s exit from Nvidia appears to have weakened confidence in the company and wider AI ecosystem. Many investors, technology sector luminaries as well as Nvidia’s own employees are now calling for Huang’s return.

Nvidia has said it is not considering inviting Huang back.

The way I see it, market regulators and corporate governance experts should begin thinking hard about how seemingly indispensable corporate leaders such as Huang can be effectively checked; and how to ensure fast-growing companies in important new fields do not betray their stakeholders.

Anthropic’s share classes

Part of the answer may come from the big AI companies themselves. Anthropic, for one, had some interesting things to say during the run-up to its initial public offering.

In a letter to prospective investors, the company’s founders extolled the potential of AI to boost productivity and accelerate the pace of medical breakthroughs, while also warning of the immense harm the technology may inflict on humanity.

“AI has unusually large externalities, both positive and negative. Cultivating the positive externalities, and defending against the negative ones, is to some degree in tension with the natural incentives of a for-profit company, and with the standard governance structure of a publicly traded company,” the founders said.

To address this, Anthropic was formed as a public benefit corporation, which requires its board to weigh the interests of its shareholders against its public benefit mission and the interests of those materially affected by its conduct.

Within that structure, different groups of stakeholders are accorded influence and interest through five different classes of shares.

Most of the control lies with holders of its Class F and Class T shares. The single Class F share, held by an entity controlled by Anthropic’s seven co-founders, has 50.1 per cent voting power.

On the other hand, an independent body called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), holds Anthropic’s single Class T share, giving it the power to appoint four of the seven members of the company’s board.

Anthropic will also issue Class E shares to its non-founder employees over time, giving them a say on some governance matters – including the appointment of one Class T director under certain circumstances.

All the economic benefits of the company belong exclusively to holders of its Class A and Class N shares, though. The difference between the two is that the Class N shares have no voting rights, except where required by law.

The Class N shares are held by Anthropic’s public benefit fund and some strategic partners, such as Amazon and Alphabet. The company plans to contribute 2 per cent of its equity to its public benefit fund for every sustained 50 per cent increase in its share price.

The Class N shares convert to Class A shares when transferred by their holders to non-affiliated parties.

Improve standard practices

Investors who resisted the introduction of dual-class shares in Singapore may well be appalled by Anthropic’s multiple share classes.

Not only will Anthropic’s founders maintain majority voting power even if they dispose of their shares, the trustees of the LTBT may appoint directors opposed to the company maximising its profits. Holders of the Class A shares will also face dilution from the ongoing issue and conversion of Class N shares.

However, Anthropic’s founders pointed out in their letter that the size and structure of the company’s plan to allocate equity to its public benefit fund is “not outside the range” of executive compensation packages at some companies.

It may also be desirable, in my view, for independent bodies of various stripes to have some influence over corporate behemoths that bestride the world.

Anthropic may be more aware of its own power than many other companies in the same league, because of the nature of its business and the fact that it has garnered a US$1.5 trillion valuation within only six years of its founding.

By contrast, Nvidia attained a market capitalisation of US$1 trillion only in 2023, three decades after it began operating. While its CEO Huang should be proud of his achievement, his stunning fall from grace is perhaps a sign that the company needs to be run differently now.

Anthropic’s novel governance framework may well not be the answer, of course – indeed, the company itself says it is a work in progress. Yet, its attempt to improve on standard corporate practices is probably something other companies should emulate as they grow and evolve.

“We will make mistakes, and we expect to learn from others as much as they learn from us. If our competitors adopt our practices and improve on them, we consider that a success,” its founders said.

data.title: âWalking a tightropeâ: OCBC CEO Tan Teck Long on balancing bold moves with conservative banking
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Nearly a year into his tenure as OCBC’s group CEO, Tan Teck Long still considers himself a “conservative” banker.

He used the word repeatedly in an interview with The Business Times, reflecting on his approach to technology, investments and regional expansion plans since taking the helm in January.

Yet, that description appears at odds with the pace of change at Singapore’s second-largest lender under his leadership.

Over the past 11 months, OCBC has acquired HSBC’s retail and wealth franchise in Indonesia; brought together the leaders of its wealth businesses into a single committee; and launched an artificial intelligence-powered banking app it called “avatar banking”.

But Tan rejects the suggestion that these moves signal a shift in the bank’s risk appetite. Rather, they reflect its ability to make calculated decisions based on a deep understanding of the risks involved.

“What we have shown is that we are nimble and we have the ability to make big moves where called for,” he said. “To us, we remain conservative because we know what we are doing.”

For Tan, protecting customer deposits and preserving trust in the brand take precedence over maximising profits, particularly in an uncertain environment. That does not mean shying away from opportunities.

“It is like walking a tightrope, because to say no to everything is very easy for risk management, but that’s not the purpose,” he said.

Against a backdrop of geopolitical uncertainty and market volatility, OCBC has embarked on its “Next Frontier” strategy – one of its most ambitious expansion plans in recent years as it positions itself to ride upcoming megatrends and improve its return on equity (ROE).

The strategy is already showing results. Its focus on wealth, in particular, led wealth fees to rise 25 per cent in the first nine months of 2026.

Tan believes double-digit growth in its wealth business should remain sustainable, given the opportunities to expand the bank’s capabilities in its other core markets of Hong Kong, Malaysia and Indonesia.

Embracing fragmentation

Asia’s fragmented markets have long challenged lenders seeking regional expansion.

While Singapore and Hong Kong serve as regional wealth hubs, OCBC’s businesses in Malaysia and Indonesia are more focused on domestic wealth accumulation.

But Tan believes these differences can work to OCBC’s advantage, enabling the bank to tailor the execution of its strategy to each market rather than adopt a one-size-fits-all approach.

While the bank sets group-wide risk and technology policies, its country management teams can work with group management to adapt them to local market conditions.

Tan joked that OCBC’s senior executives have to work four times harder than their counterparts at foreign banks, given the need to adapt to four distinct markets.

“It’s a huge competitive advantage,” he said, “because the foreign banks (operating in many more locations) will not be able to react this way.”

With just four core markets, the bank is also “rightsized” to adapt its approach. This allows for a more efficient allocation of resources, as the solutions are more suited to the needs of the individual market rather than a blanket adoption of policies, Tan explained.

OCBC’s expansion plans reflect these differences.

Across its Singapore-Hong Kong twin hubs, the lender aims to deliver an integrated banking, wealth and insurance proposition, including services catered to ageing populations. In Hong Kong, it also plans to expand its affluent segment and global markets business.

As for Malaysia, the bank is looking to expand its affluent customer base through Great Eastern Malaysia’s ecosystem, capture inbound investment flows and pursue opportunities arising from initiatives such as the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone.

Meanwhile, in Indonesia, the lender aims to grow its private bank.

Tan expects that these will come together and enable OCBC to accelerate growth across its four core markets, even as their different characteristics call for distinct approaches.

This flexibility also extends to his leadership style, which he describes as “situational”. Where he believes employees are capable of resolving problems independently, he prefers giving them the autonomy to do so.

“When you give (the team) that bandwidth and latitude to sort (problems) out, then they will start to surface things which haven’t occurred to me,” he said.

Balancing growth and risk

Technology is another important area that underpins Tan’s strategy.

Rather than adopting AI for its own sake, he wants the bank to redesign workflows first, deploying the technology only when it can improve processes and ultimately lift revenue and ROE.

“I have been asked by some analysts how much benefit I get from AI,” he said. “But why do I want to count the benefits of AI when I should be getting benefits at scale end-to-end through a better process, and the better process actually enables me to plug in the latest AI tool, which is fit for purpose?”

Tan is also reluctant to incur additional costs simply to quantify AI’s standalone contribution, particularly when improvements stem from a combination of process redesign, digitalisation and AI.

“By not succumbing to the pressure to go and measure it, I actually now have more money to do the right things,” he said.

Instead, OCBC is pursuing what he calls an “expertise-led” approach, bringing together banking, technology and data specialists to redesign workflows and identify where AI can deliver business value.

The bank still tracks the usage of its AI solutions internally, alongside broader business outcomes.

One example of its technology ambitions is avatar banking, through an AI-powered avatar banking app to give wealth advice.

Tan said that OCBC is the only bank in South-east Asia to offer such an AI-native banking channel, with the platform currently in beta testing as the bank refines its capabilities.

The lender is taking a more measured approach when it comes to product improvements, as it seeks to minimise the risk of AI hallucinations and ensure that the information provided to clients is appropriate.

Looking ahead, he believes that OCBC is still at the early stages of its strategy shift. He hopes for the bank to progress more quickly, but he also noted the need to balance revenue growth with service improvements.

He also flagged cybersecurity risks as one of his biggest worries given the pace of technological change.

Ultimately, the challenge for Tan will be to balance OCBC’s growth and transformation without compromising the conservative approach to risk that he considers fundamental to the bank.

“How do we walk a tightrope? We (have to) build our capabilities and understanding, and then walk the tightrope.”

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: COP31 climate talks collapse as EU and others reject deal
data.description:
[ANTALYA] UN climate talks ended in collapse on Sunday (Nov 22) as the EU and others rejected a final deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkey and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

The failed talks reflect the struggle by governments across the world to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change – including heatwaves, wildfires, floods and powerful storms – as wars and economic pressures compete for their attention.

More than two weeks of negotiations spilled two days into overtime, making it the longest COP on record, and yet a deal was elusive.

“There is nothing to do. We did all that we could,” Turkey’s conference president Murat Kurum told the closing plenary, saying he would not advance any new text. He later left the stage even though country representatives were still delivering speeches.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s COP31 president of negotiations, said the outcome “very disappointing” and that disagreements over fossil fuels and climate finance had been obstacles to a deal.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was also dismayed. “I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” he said.

The last time United Nations climate talks failed to get a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009. While many recent COP summits have been fraught, they have provided important signals for business investment and provided a spur for advances in renewable power and electric vehicle technology, analysts say.

Arguably, they have also helped to curb warming.

When countries in 2015 struck the Paris Agreement, which included an aspiration to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, projections suggested existing policies put the world on course for roughly 4 deg C of warming this century. A decade later, the prognosis is 2.8 deg C.

This year’s COP is the first since the UN’s environmental body in October confirmed the rise in global temperatures was set to overshoot 1.5 deg C, a level beyond which scientists say extreme weather impacts intensify.

No mention of fossil fuels

Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O’Brien said the EU could not support the proposed deal in part because it made no mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say drive global warming.

“It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels,” he said.

Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing countries have said that fossil fuels will play a role in the economy for the foreseeable future, and it lobbied to keep any mention of fossil fuels out of the text, observers at the summit said.

The failed deal had acknowledged the planet’s projected temperature overshoot and called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it, something oil-producing countries had been keen to include.

Scientists say removing carbon from the atmosphere – when paired with steep emissions cuts – is vital to avoiding the worst impacts of climate change, but critics of the proposed deal said they were worried the carbon removal language would be used as a licence to keep pumping oil.

A representative for the Saudi delegation told the summit at the closing plenary that he was surprised at the resistance to what he said was a concrete solution to global warming.

Developing countries had also criticised the deal for not providing sufficient climate finance to help them adapt to a warming planet. The deal had called for a tripling of such finance, but did not specify from what baseline.

It had also included a goal put forward by Turkey to expand electricity’s share of total final world energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, from around 23 per cent now.

Proponents of that pledge said it could cut greenhouse gas emissions by speeding the transition away from fuel-powered cars, furnaces, and other equipment. But critics said it could force more costs onto poor nations without providing a clear path away from fossil fuels.

The COP process is the main vehicle through which countries coordinate their efforts to curb global warming. Its annual meeting provides an opportunity for nations to signal they are willing to work together to find solutions and help finance the problems rising temperatures cause.

The failure to agree a political declaration in Antalya does not erase the obligations agreed by previous UN conferences.

Belgium’s Minister of Mobility, Climate, and Ecological Transition Jean-Luc Crucke said it was a difficult outcome, but “not the end of multilateralism”. “There has to be courage to say no,” he said. REUTERS

data.title: Chinese exchanges ease margin trading requirements to aid stock markets
data.description:
[SHANGHAI] China’s three main stock exchanges announced plans to aid struggling share prices with a batch of measures such as easing requirements for margin financing.

In addition, the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses unveiled plans for fee reductions to lower trading costs, while the Shenzhen exchange also proposed to introduce a market-making mechanism in its startup board ChiNext.

The moves came after Beijing unveiled measures in early November to encourage share purchases as equities struggle amid sluggish growth at home, a global sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks and rising geopolitical tensions.

The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index dropped nearly 3 per cent during the week starting Nov 9 to hit a 16-month low. Shanghai’s tech-heavy Star Market and Shenzhen’s ChiNext have both tumbled more than 40 per cent from their June peaks.

Regulatory changes

The Chinese measures come as other Asian markets including South Korea and Taiwan respond to stock market jitters with regulatory changes designed to steady volatility.

Under the new rules announced by the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges, investors can borrow more money to buy stocks against the same collateral.

Starting Nov 30, the minimum margin ratio would be cut to 80 per cent from 100 per cent previously, in a reversal of a policy announced in January.

“Margin financing activity has weakened significantly recently, while overall leverage is low,” the three exchanges said.

The cut in margin requirements “would improve market liquidity and support the market’s long-term stability and healthy development”.

Measures aim to boost market confidence

The level of China’s outstanding margin loans has dropped more than 20 per cent to roughly 2.2 trillion yuan (US$329.5 billion), from a peak of three trillion yuan in late June.

Separately, the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges announced fee cuts aiming to lower trading costs, boost market confidence and invigorate the market.

The Shenzhen bourse also published draft rules to introduce market-making mechanisms in a bid to “curb share price swings, improve pricing efficiency and strengthen market resilience”. REUTERS

data.title: Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers
data.description:
[NEW YORK] For the second time in 2026, Wall Street bankers and lawyers took home a massive pay cheque from a record-setting initial public offering.

And for the second time in 2026, some of them came out of it complaining in private about how the process was riddled with complications, and unlike any they had worked on before.

With SpaceX’s IPO in June, in which banks earned half a billion US dollars in fees, bankers chafed over how tightly the Elon Musk-led company controlled the months-long process and kept financial and other information private, making it hard for advisers to do their jobs.

As Anthropic’s IPO, dubbed internally “Project Lantern”, eclipsed SpaceX on Thursday (Nov 19) and bankers took home more than half a billion US dollars in fees, several people close to the process listed a litany of problems that had plagued the offering process.

This included a compressed timeline, marred by last-minute changes and delays in sharing financial projections; rushed document approvals; and highly unusual restrictions on bankers and concern about leaks – especially after Reuters reported many details from a draft IPO filing weeks before it was made public.

Anthropic, for example, instructed some of its 22 IPO underwriters to limit the number of bankers working on the deal to four, asking the companies to make sure they were senior staff, several people familiar with the matter said.

One of the people said the restriction likely came out of fear that information would leak, and that the banks found a way to work around it anyway.

Underlying these complaints is a new power dynamic between tech companies and Wall Street.

Companies such as SpaceX, Anthropic – and potentially OpenAI in the future – have come to wield enormous power as the transformative potential of artificial intelligence creates a frenzied demand for their shares, and they are wielding it to do things their way.

That is upsetting some bankers. But banks and investors appear to have little choice but to play along.

“These companies certainly did have some market power to tell underwriters that it’s not going to be business as usual,” said Jay Ritter, a University of Florida professor emeritus who researches IPOs.

“But the big Wall Street firms, I suspect, are still going to be doing things as business as usual for all but maybe OpenAI (after these two deals).”

He added that both SpaceX and Anthropic had negotiated to pay underwriters nothing on the additional shares sold through the greenshoe option.

“I don’t think most companies are going to be able to demand zero spread on overallotment shares,” he said.

Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the two lead underwriters on the two IPOs, declined to comment.

SpaceX and OpenAI did not respond to queries.

Both SpaceX and Anthropic debuted successfully, raising record amounts of money, and their shares rallied initially.

A key part of the underwriters’ job is to market the securities. Due to the demand for AI, that was an easy sell; both companies had order books oversubscribed many times over.

After an initial burst in shares, the trajectories of the two big AI companies diverged.

SpaceX climbed to a post-listing peak of US$201.80 on Jun 16, before retreating below its US$135 IPO price for the first time in mid-July.

Anthropic’s shares closed down 8.5 per cent on Friday after a 17 per cent first-day pop, as a dramatic unravelling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.

Unusual non-competes and restrictions

In the case of SpaceX’s IPO, the people close to the process said Musk’s team dictated terms at every stage.

His team told the largest and most powerful US banks – including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley – how to market SpaceX’s stock and to whom.

It told some banks the specific order sizes they needed to “fill”, in some cases a few billion US dollars, and gave them instructions on what types of investors to bring. Banks signed on to underwrite the IPO without being told what they would be paid, the people said.

The underlying current running through Anthropic’s IPO process was a sense of extreme caution, as interpreted by several of the people who spoke to Reuters.

Anthropic asked some senior officers at banks working on its IPO to sign legal documents restricting core members of the transaction team from working with rival companies, including OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek and Hugging Face, for six months after it went public, said the people.

Banks routinely manage conflicts and protect client confidentiality. But bankers and lawyers said it is rare for an IPO to impose exclusivity this broad, particularly on individual bankers.

In previous head-to-head IPOs such as those of ride-sharing rivals Uber and Lyft, or real-estate companies Trulia and Zillow, banks could simply pick a side, in part because the deals were smaller and required fewer banks.

Anthropic, by contrast, needed a broad syndicate to raise the enormous amount of capital it was seeking. That, some of the people said, explained why Anthropic sought to bind individual bankers with these restrictions.

One banker who declined to sign on to the agreement said it was a challenge to find people who could promise not to actively cover or engage with Anthropic’s peers, especially as several of those companies pursue their own initial or secondary offerings.

Information leaks and late nights

Some of the restrictions were meant to control leaks of information.

Nearly four weeks before Anthropic’s filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), called Form S-1, was made public, Reuters reported on it, revealing details of the company’s financials, risk factors, dealings with other tech companies and other information.

Anthropic also used a product called NetRoadshow to share information, instead of regular PDFs, with most of the banks underwriting the deal.

NetRoadshow logs access details, including information such as who has seen the document and looked at which page. Documents on NetRoadshow also had individual bankers’ names as watermarks.

Leaks continued to surface in the press, but using NetRoadshow complicated bankers’ work, also because the platform would not let them save copies of documents, one of the people said.

Anthropic planned to file an updated securities filing – called an S-1A – with the SEC with the price range and to launch the marketing on Nov 10. To do so, it needed to send a draft to all the banks in its syndicate for them to sign off on it.

The night before it was to happen, a law firm on the deal sent a PDF to the banks about the sale of shares in Canada.

But soon, it followed up with another e-mail asking them to disregard it, saying it “contains incorrect price range and share information”, going by the e-mail, which was seen by Reuters.

The correct S-1A was then sent via the NetRoadshow platform around 2 am New York time. Banks were told they had several hours to sign off on it before it was filed with the SEC. REUTERS
